en: Table of Contents for the Essential Knowledge of the Two Orders of the Forest Monasteries:
General Introduction;
West Order.
Essentials for the Head Seat (applicable to the West Hall); Essentials for the Secretary;
Essentials for the Librarian; Essentials for the Guest Master;
Essentials for the Bath Master (including the Inner Latrine Attendant); Essentials for the Abbot’s Attendant.
The Head Monk of the Eastern Wing must know; the Rector must know;
the Assistant Administrator must know; the Chief Cook must know.
The Head of the Monastery (Zhísuì) must know this; the Two Orders of the Forest Community must know this.
Written by Xíngyuán, disciple of the Abbot Tōngróng of Jīnslù Temple.

The *Chanyuan Qinggui* (Pure Rules of Baizhang) is cited as a whole because it governs the abbot, the two orders of officers, and the various assemblies alike. Why, then, are only the two orders singled out here?
It is because while the *Qinggui* provides the general framework for the two orders, the specific details regarding personal conduct and the execution of duties are addressed therein.

It is subtle; there is still much that has not yet been fully perfected. Generally, the establishment of the two orders is for the sake of managing affairs for the community, so that they may support one another like arms and elbows, acting as mutual bulwarks to adorn the imperial legacy with patterns of black and white, ensuring its greatness and endurance.

As for those who manage the treasury and granaries and attend to all secular and spiritual affairs, becoming proficient in both worldly and transcendent matters, such individuals will, in the future, occupy positions of authority and be honored as masters.

When presiding over the assembly or governing affairs, one must also know the origins of the long-established and unchanging regulations that may be followed as before, thereby clarifying that they possess a fundamental basis.
This is precisely why it is said that whether one perfects oneself or others depends on this.

One who understands this intent will not feel resentment even if the positions of east and west are reversed, nor will they be concerned with the hierarchy of rank when advancing or withdrawing according to the occasion.

They calculated their duties according to gain and loss; each attended to their own occupation and each settled in their own dwelling. Above, there was no heart of dissatisfaction; below, there were no dissenting opinions. How harmonious!
It is for this reason that the scholars of antiquity sighed, saying that the dignified decorum of the Three Dynasties is rarely seen even here, and it is truly worthy of praise.
Yet, as the ages have passed from prosperity to decline, human sentiments have become lax and changed. Some stubbornly cling to their own views with self-conceit, or...

They remain in a state of bewildered neglect; or, with strengths and weaknesses at odds, factions engage in mutual strife; or, through disputes over right and wrong, they fail to maintain harmony for the entire year.
This not only stains the Dharma assembly, but moreover fails to contribute to the Vinaya. For these reasons, I have selected its major outlines.

Having examined these minute details and compiled them into formal articles, I have titled this work "What Must Be Known" (Xuzhi). Whether it be understood by me as a virtue or condemned by me as a fault, what excuse could I possibly offer?
— West Hall.
According to the protocol for the Abbot’s ascent to the hall, those of the West Order (Xi-xu) are listed first.
All who hold positions within the two orders ought to constantly consult the "Mirror" (Guijian) of their respective quarters and diligently practice their duties to support the Dharma seat together.
If one becomes lax or neglects these matters, the rules and regulations will not be sustained, and the monastic community (Conglin) will be brought to ruin; such would be the fault.
This is no trivial matter; I hope you will examine it with care so as not to cause any failure in the affairs of the monastery. My most earnest request.
*Shouzuo Xuzhi* (General Rules for the Head Seat, applicable to the West Hall).
Now, the existence of the head seat (*shouzuo*) in a Chan monastery is like the collar on a garment or the main cord in a net. It is the collar and the main cord.
It is here that the fundamental source of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, the eyes of humanity and the heavens, and the exemplary conduct of the monastic community are all centered.
Therefore, those who hold this office must value honoring their superiors and loving their subordinates, taking it as their own responsibility to uphold the Great Dharma.

Should they, however, act with improper conduct or fail to exercise restraint in the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, they will lose the respect of both the internal and external communities; how then could they illuminate the past and support the future? For this reason...
I have established several articles as a mirror for this very quarters, hoping that there may be those who arise in succession to follow them and practice accordingly,
so that there shall be no cause for concern regarding the failure of the undertaking.
The abbot has life; those who act on his behalf should be careful not to bring disgrace upon him.
One should report back on whether the various tasks entrusted by the abbot, both great and small, have been carried out.
In all matters, observe the regulations; do not rely on your office to indulge your own whims.
In all matters, deliberate until what is appropriate is found, and only then act.
What is spoken must not be uttered recklessly; what is done must surely reflect what was spoken.
Maintain the proper order between the honorable and the humble; be modest and humble toward others, and do not rely on your office to give rise to arrogance.
Be impartial and fair in all affairs; be broad-minded and magnanimous, and do not be biased, narrow-minded, or shallow. Do not disparage yourself.
The administrative officers of each quarters must coordinate matters both great and small; they must not establish separate households or divisions, nor give rise to feelings of "self" versus "other.
Within the hall, the *vinaya-dhara* (rector), the *shuji* (secretary), and others must show mutual understanding and respect, valuing unity and cooperation.
Do not rely on your positions to harbor private interests, thereby causing inequality among those of high and low status.

If a member of the assembly commits an offense against the hall regulations, the *karmadāna* shall call him forth. Depending on the gravity of the offense, he should be punished according to reason and consideration of circumstances.

When the *karmadāna* proposes a punishment for a member of the assembly, he must have previously consulted with and reached a consensus on the matter; he must not alter his position or change his insistence at the last moment. They should [act] in mutual accord.
In the *Kangling* (Hall of Exalted Purity), for those among the assembly in the various quarters outside the hall who violate the Pure Rules (*qinggui*), the Guest Prefect shall bring them forth;
they shall then be punished according to reason and circumstance, based on the gravity of the offense.
Whenever there are matters involving entanglements or complications that cannot be resolved through appropriate division or settlement,
one should go to the guest prefect’s quarters and consult with the assembly and the head officials to deliberate and reach a decision.
Please request the Abbot to ascend the hall for a small discourse (*xiao can*). All various administrative affairs shall follow established custom.
Morning and evening liturgical recitations must not be neglected, and all shall attend the hall for the two daily meals of rice and congee, except in cases where special circumstances apply.
During the three periods of silent retreat (*sanzhan zhijing*), one should sit with the assembly during the incense periods unless there is a specific reason for absence.
During communal labor (*puching*), one should likewise follow the assembly unless there is a specific reason for absence.

One must cherish and protect the monastery’s permanent property and utensils; do not intentionally or frivolously incur unnecessary expenses, except for those matters prescribed by established regulations.
One must not privately accept disciples or indiscriminately bestow Dharma names. Should there be those who sincerely seek refuge, permission to admit them must be requested from the Abbot.
Matters such as providing relief for the elderly and infirm, or conducting funeral rites for the deceased, shall all be carried out in consultation with the assembly.
All items belonging to the permanent endowment of this hall should be registered in a ledger for the purpose of future reference.
On the day of departure following a leave of absence, one shall clearly inventory the hall’s permanent assets according to the ledger and hand them over to the guest master (zhikè) for custody,
ensuring they do not fall into disorder.
Regarding the several points above, those in charge should each examine them closely when faced with specific matters and take initiative in putting them into practice;

there is no need to wait for oral instructions from the Abbot. Should there be any items that have not been fully detailed, I hope you will always exercise understanding accordingly. This is the admonition.
On the [day] of the [month] of the [year], established by [Name], Abbot of [Mountain Name].
Regarding the scribe:

one must know that while the renowned masters of antiquity took it as their primary responsibility to uphold the Great Dharma, they specifically requested others for calligraphy and literary composition.
The scribe records this by virtue of his office. One must know that the duties of a scribe are by no means insignificant.
Huanglong at Letan and Dahui at Zhaojue are the most prominent examples of this. Yet, to this day, the Buddha-dharma has not flourished and the social mores are not as they were in antiquity;
even if such titles exist, they are preserved merely as historical relics. Therefore, I have established several points to clarify [the matter].

This shall serve as a model for the resident monks of this monastery, so that those who succeed to these duties in the future may also exert themselves to practice it and not treat their studies lightly.

When the Abbot receives an official summons, all the memorial petitions and letters of thanks submitted on his behalf shall be handled by the Acting Administrator; this was a grand tradition of antiquity, though it is no longer practiced today.
[This is] for reference (it is appropriate to preserve it).
Regarding the collective letters and correspondence of the abbot, as well as replies to inquiries, congratulations, and condolences, the current representative shall act on his behalf;
as soon as the draft is completed, it shall be presented for approval. If the abbot has sufficient capacity, he need not involve himself in these matters.
Record the formal discourses given upon ascending the hall (*shàngtáng*), the informal sermons (*xiǎocān*), and the general dharma talks delivered in the open quarters (*kāishì*).

If the Chief Seat (*fāngzhàng*) or the Secretary Attendant (*shūzhuàng shìzhě*) is absent, the incumbent shall act as their representative. This includes the temple’s official notices, proclamations, and memorial petitions for vegetarian feasts; the formats for correspondence sent and received; and the ritual texts for prayers regarding floods, droughts, and locust plagues.
Regarding terminology: everything belongs to this category.
As for transcription, you should apply your mind with care, valuing clarity and legibility; do not write in a careless or hurried manner merely to get the task finished.
As for the four treasures of the study, their dimensions are provided by the monastery’s permanent endowment; you should cherish and protect them, and must not use them wastefully.
Regarding all matters, great and small, entrusted by the Abbot, one must report whether they have been carried out or not.

The administrative officers of the various quarters must communicate with one another on both major and minor points; they must not establish separate households or divisions, nor give rise to feelings of "us" versus "them."
When among the assembly, one should value broad-mindedness and harmony. One must not rely on one’s office to act haughtily toward superiors or to oppress subordinates.
Among the various senior and junior officials, one must not interfere in matters outside of one’s own duties, except when making requests or attending meetings for official business.
Morning and evening, one should join the assembly for chanting and recitation, as well as attend the hall for the two daily meals of rice and congee, unless there is a specific reason for otherwise.
At the third board, when silence is observed, one should sit with the assembly during the incense period, except in cases of necessity.
When participating in communal labor (*fushō*), one should follow the assembly, except when there are specific duties to attend to.
All official documents and utensils belonging to the permanent endowment (*jōzō*) of one’s own quarters should be privately recorded in a register for the purpose of future reference and inspection.
On the day of retirement, one shall clearly inventory the monastery’s permanent documents and utensils according to the register and hand them over to the new secretary for custody;
they must not be allowed to become disordered.
Regarding the several points above, those in charge should each examine them closely when confronted with actual matters and act accordingly according to their respective roles.
Should there be any items that are not fully detailed, we hope you will exercise understanding and adapt them to the circumstances as needed. This is the instruction.
On the [day] of the [month] of the [year], established by the Abbot of Mount [Name].

The Sūtra Repository must be known by its custodian: it is the magnificent repository where the life-vein of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is entrusted. Those who hold its charge must value diligence and meticulousness above all else.
The mind should take the protection and upholding of the holy teachings as its primary concern.
If the study desk is not kept solemn and clamor is not ceased, it will not be the way for a Librarian (Zangzhu) to attend to the assembly.

Therefore, I have established several articles to serve as a mirror for this very office, so that those who hold this post in the future may likewise rely upon and practice them, rather than neglecting their duties with mere formalities.
All the scriptures contained within the canon should be treated with reverence.
The scriptures within the canon should be arranged according to their title numbers in sequential order, so as to facilitate consultation.
Regarding the number of volumes and cases of the scriptures within the Tripiṭaka, they should be placed in a specific location and a general register must be established for easy reference.

As for the scriptures within the Tripiṭaka that have become damp or damaged by insects, they must be carefully tended to and dried at the proper time (this refers to either during periods of mold or in the sixth month).
Furthermore, as the task of drying and roasting is laborious, it is advisable to request the assistance of others.
One must constantly cross-reference all the scriptures within the treasury against their catalogs;
for those that are fragmented or missing, they must be mended and supplemented.

Regarding the scriptures within the treasury: whenever anyone requests to borrow them for perusal, their names shall be recorded in the register. Upon completion of the reading, they must be returned;
furthermore, they shall be checked against the register and re-entered into the treasury so as not to be lost or scattered.
Those in charge of the scriptures within the treasury should also apply themselves with diligence to extensive research and broaden their knowledge and experience;
do not merely treat them as antiquities.
The locks and keys of the scriptural treasury must be strictly guarded.
Cleanse the treasury hall and thoroughly wipe down the tables and desks.
Regarding all matters, large and small, entrusted by the Abbot, you must report back on whether they have been carried out.
When among the assembly, one should value broad-mindedness and harmony. One must not rely on one's office to act haughtily toward superiors or to oppress subordinates.

Those serving as officials in various quarters should communicate on matters both great and small; they must not establish separate households or divisions, nor give rise to feelings of "us" versus "them."
The various quarters, both large and small, must not interfere in the affairs of others, except when summoned for official business or meetings.
All items belonging to the permanent endowment of one’s own quarter should be recorded privately in a ledger for the purpose of future reference and inspection.

On the date of retirement, the current resident monks shall clearly inventory and verify, according to their respective numbers, all items belonging to this monastery as well as the cases and volumes of the scriptures within the library, and hand them over to the new librarian for custody; they must not be allowed to become disordered.
Regarding the several points above, those in charge should each examine them closely when the occasion arises and proceed accordingly ahead of time.
Should there be any items that are not fully detailed, we only hope for your understanding and flexibility at all times. This is the instruction.
Established by [Name], Abbot of [Mountain Name], on the [Day] of the [Month] of the [Year].
The Guest Prefect (Kichaku)须知 (Must Know):

The Guest Prefect serves as the vital link and binding cord of the monastic community (*sōrin*), acting as the eyes and ears for its external protectors. Unless one is profoundly talented, capable, upright, and commanding respect, one cannot fulfill this role.
The position of *zhong* (attendant) is not easily assumed; it is like Xuedou’s tenure at Taiyang or Chan Yue’s at Shishuang.
As for those who harbor animosity toward the poor and reverence the wealthy, or who value the laity while disparaging the monastics—how can they be said to know the way of the *zhike*?
Therefore, I have established several articles as a mirror for this office, so that future incumbents may rely upon them in their conduct.
One must ensure there are no apprehensions of failure.

When officials in office arrive at the mountain monastery, the protocols for their reception and escort must first be discussed with the Prior and finalized with the Abbot before they are implemented.

When an official in office visits the mountain monastery, one must first consult with the Prior and the Head of the Kitchen regarding the preparation of a certain number of vegetarian meals, as well as a certain number of items such as hot soup, glutinous rice cakes, and fruit dishes. Only after reporting this to the Abbot should the preparations proceed.

Furthermore, the official’s quarters, bedding, curtains, utensils, incense, candles, firewood, charcoal, and other such items must be carefully attended to and protected. Upon reaching the time for the meal—

The hot dishes and food shall be inspected according to the prescribed ritual. Those accompanying them, such as the *zaoke* (black-clad runners) and others, shall likewise be settled in their designated quarters.

They shall be entertained with vegetarian meals and tea, ensuring that no one is neglected or left out (if officials are on the road, they shall be specifically provided with vegetarian meals and tea; the specific protocols for such occasions shall be determined according to the circumstances).

When officials, patrons, or venerable elders arrive at the mountain monastery, one must first dispatch an attendant to prepare a clean quarters, arranging for bedding, curtains, utensils, lamps, oil, and other necessities, remaining on call to provide service. Upon their arrival, they shall be welcomed with tea and soup.
If one wishes to visit the Abbot, one must first notify him in advance; thereafter, he will lead the visitor up for an audience.
If one wishes to visit the Head Seat, the Treasury Office, the various quarters, or to pay respects at other locations as one pleases, the Abbot shall personally escort them there.
When government officials, lay patrons, or venerable elders visit the abbot’s quarters, the *zhishi* (administrative officer) shall first be instructed to prepare the seating arrangements.
The sequence for serving tea must follow the established ritual; no deviation or lapse in propriety is permitted.

Officials, donors, and venerable elders should always attend to and supervise the morning and midday meals, as well as the morning and evening tea and soup, ensuring they are served at the proper times.
When officials, donors, or lay practitioners arrive at the mountain, or on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month, they should wait for the assembly to complete their recitations.
Once the inspection of the quarters is completed, one must ensure that all the invited head officials arrive together at the guest hall for an audience;

only then does one not fail the great principles of the monastic community. If a guest of high rank arrives very early and has not yet been able to join the assembly, it is convenient to arrange the meeting at dawn.
Next, when monks or lay guests arrive at the mountain, the serving of meals and tea shall be conducted according to the usual regulations.

If they wish to visit the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*), the various administrative offices (*liáo*), or to attend the hall (*candáng*) and settle into their quarters (*anshān*), they should also be escorted there. Alternatively, if there is someone designated to guide them to their assigned quarters, one should simply observe the circumstances and not be overly rigid in following this rule.
When female lay guests arrive at the mountain monastery, they must be accommodated in the guest hall for women; they must not be allowed to mingle with the monastics.
When honored guests arrive at the mountain, the rector (karmadāna) shall also accompany them to provide supervision and care. This should be understood.
Whenever important guests arrive at the mountain monastery, those who require high-quality delicacies and vegetables should instruct the steward (kusi) and the head cook (dianzuo) to prepare them.

When a donor hosts a vegetarian feast and invites the abbot to ascend the hall for a sermon, the guest should first be led to the Abbot’s Quarters (shangfang). Once the formal meeting and greetings are concluded, [the ceremony may proceed].

Lead the way to the storehouse. Prepare the ritual for the offering meal (*zhāiyí*). Once the rituals for ascending the hall (*shàngtáng*) and inviting the assembly of head officers (*tóushǒu*) are completed, instruct an attendant to follow with a tray.
Lead the patron (*zhāizhǔ*) to the meditation hall (*cāntáng*) and the various quarters (*liáo*) to present gifts. Then, speak as follows:

The donor [Name], for the sake of a certain matter, requests that the Venerable Master ascend the hall on a certain day. Once the offerings have been completed, he again instructs an attendant to go to the Abbot’s quarters to arrange the ceremonial protocols.
The donor holds incense and waits in attendance, joining the assembly of heads of departments in making the earnest request.

On the following day, he visits the abbot’s quarters two or three times, performing the same rites as before (or, if the administrative staff is too busy with their duties to manage the protocol, it is permissible for them first to lead the patron in his invitation, after which they distribute the invitations themselves;

furthermore, if the patron has not yet met the abbot but immediately prepares the ritual implements to extend the invitation, one should simply observe the circumstances and not be bound by these rules).
When a donor prepares a vegetarian feast (zhāi) to present offerings before the Buddha, they must first enter the hall and inform the *weina* (ritual director).

Thereafter, they lead the donor to hold incense and wait in attendance, following the sequence according to the ritual protocol without the slightest omission. (If there is a general offering, the drum is struck three times and the assembly gathers together.)

At the time of the meal, the abbot must lead the donor in holding the incense. The abbot proceeds to the invitation hall, and once the incumbent has come out and taken his seat, the various head officials complete their prostrations.
Then, the donor is instructed to face the incumbent, raise the incense, and perform three prostrations;

subsequently, they must also prostrate to the assembly of the two orders (East and West). (If the donor is particularly devout, the ritual offerings for the meal should be personally handed over; in this case, the attendant official should be ordered to hold a tray and wait nearby. Otherwise, proceed according to the standard protocol. Furthermore...
When the meal is finished, the abbot shall escort the host of the vegetarian feast (zhāizhǔ) to see him off; this should be understood as a proper practice, though it need not be strictly observed.

When the donor provides the feast and distributes the monetary offerings (shànqìn), if they are pressed for time, the assistant administrator (fùsì) should be authorized to act on their behalf. Furthermore, regarding the distribution of the offerings, there are various methods such as equal division or unequal allocation;
these should be adjusted according to the circumstances.
When a donor arrives at the mountain to provide a vegetarian feast, one must calculate the thickness of their resources and inform the Vice Abbot in advance;
provisions should be prepared according to the circumstances without being bound by rigid formalism.
If visiting monks from other regions come to seek an audience with the Abbot and do not bring ceremonial gifts, they should be granted an audience;
one must not treat them with dissatisfaction or delay, thereby violating the principles of propriety.
Regarding all matters large and small entrusted by the Abbot, one must report back on whether they have been carried out.
When the Abbot invites honored guests for tea or when the Guest Hall conducts formal audiences, one must provide timely supervision so as not to fail in the display of propriety.
For the constant provision of tea during the *zhāi* (fasting) periods, it is appropriate for the *jiànsì* (superintendent) to join in inviting the *fāngwǎng* (abbot).

In the event that the office of the *jiànsì* is vacant, or when he is away on other business—such as matters concerning estate lands, tax deeds, or the formal protocol of receiving and seeing off guests—the same applies.

Regarding the assignment of duties for congratulations and condolences, as well as all matters of vital importance at various locations, the administrative office (Kusō) shall deliberate together and act as proxies.

Every night, after the minor period of silence has ended, they shall go to the treasury room and, together with the Chief Administrator (Jianyuan) and the Head of Quarters (Zhishuai), manage affairs and deliberate on the day’s activities for the following morning.

Whenever a new head official (*shoushou*) is appointed, they shall be led to pay respects to the Abbot, visit the Hall for Monks (*cantang*), and tour the various quarters (*xunliao*). Following this, they shall be invited for tea.
When a head official or administrative officer is about to depart on official business or take leave, they must inform the *kusisi* (the administrative office) in advance;

the office shall provide them with a vegetarian feast, tea, and light refreshments as a send-off. Upon rising the following morning, the formal meal shall be served according to protocol, followed by side dishes and tea.
Regarding fruits: those to be kept for use while traveling should be inspected and prepared as needed according to the occasion.

In all matters concerning the sentiments of incoming and outgoing guests, as well as the senior and junior officials within the monastery who have rendered service to the permanent estate (chángzhù), when they request leave to depart the mountain, it is appropriate to perform the rite of parting gifts; this must be deliberated upon and reported to the Abbot (fāngzhàng).

The head of the *kāolak* (provisioning office) shall remain in permanent charge, ensuring that he understands the specific invitations for each location. Together with the storekeeper (*kūzǐ*), they shall arrange the food and provide hospitality.

When the retreat concludes at the end of the two seasons of spring and winter, they must pre-arrange for the invitation of the fundraising master (*huàzhǔ*), which must be discussed and decided upon jointly with the Chief Administrator (*jiānyuàn*) before submitting the formal report.
The Abbot:

According to the annual custom, the distribution of rice for the midday meal must be prepared in a timely manner. Furthermore, one must appoint those who shall receive the rice for the following year.
As for the members of the various quarters within the hall who have requested leave to depart from the mountain, you should inquire in detail as to their reasons and examine them.
They shall come and go as necessary to deliberate upon matters of admission or dismissal.
For resident monks and newly arrived monastics who earnestly request entry into the hall, they must first be led to pay their respects to the Abbot in advance.
Distribute the individual tickets. Then, place them into the *baizhi* (white ticket) register.
For those among the assembly in the various quarters outside the hall who become impatient and request to leave, you should encourage and comfort them.
When they have generated the aspiration for the Way, if the number reaches its limit, others shall be selected to fill the vacancies.
The names of all those in the various quarters outside the hall who are part of the monastic community must be recorded on the water-tables, so that they may be assigned and rotated as needed.
Regarding the various minor attendants in the individual quarters outside the Hall: if there is a vacancy in an office, the assembly should be requested to appoint a replacement.

Regarding the practitioners in the individual quarters outside the Hall who act contrary to the community or whose conduct warrants expulsion: they shall be deliberated upon and reported to the Abbot.
If among the practitioners in any of the quarters there are disputes or slanderous talk, one should mediate and resolve them based on reason, lest they lead to further complications.
If any practitioner in any of the quarters is performing labor or is ill, one should inquire after them morning and evening regarding their hunger, thirst, cold, and heat.
The administrative officers of each quarters must coordinate matters both large and small; they shall not establish separate households or divisions, nor give rise to notions of "self" and "other.
They shall not focus solely on their own duties while neglecting communal affairs or evading responsibility, thereby causing dissatisfaction among their fellow residents.
When among the multitude, one should value broad-mindedness and harmony. One must not rely on one's office to act haughtily toward superiors or to oppress subordinates.
Should there be those among the assembly who offend me, I should contemplate their hardships and toil;
I must not harbor resentment or conceal private grievances, but must certainly reform their errors before desisting.

Instructing and admonishing them with understanding and compliance, one must not rashly employ the whip, physical blows, or harsh and venomous speech. It is appropriate to treat them with thorough consideration and skillful harmony;
do not rely on your position to bully them, thereby causing them to resign out of a sense of neglect.
Regarding the guest quarters and dormitories: instruct the attendants (*zhishui*) to sweep them clean every morning and not to indulge in laziness.
They must take care of the beds, curtains, quilts, mats, utensils, and other furnishings, guarding against damage.

Should anything be kept improperly, instruct the attendants to wash or sun it immediately, ensuring that all matters are handled appropriately (for example, in the fourth month, one should collect and sun the cotton batting, and thoroughly wash the quilted covers).

Repairing guest tents; sun-drying clean straw mats; and at the end of autumn and the beginning of winter, sun-drying dry grass thatch, washing clean quilted covers, and storing away items such as cotton batting.
Guest quarters, beds, curtains, bedding, mats, utensils, and other articles should be recorded item by item in a register for the purpose of inspection and verification.
All items belonging to the guest rooms shall be ordered to be packed and stored accordingly to prevent loss.

Regarding all bedding and articles within the guest quarters: whenever anyone borrows items from any of the inner or outer lodgings, regardless of size, they must record their names in the register and maintain constant supervision over them, so that they may be returned promptly and not lost.
If there are any missing items of small or large size in the guest rooms, the White Treasury Officer shall be notified in advance to procure replacements for future use.
When boats enter or depart, one must ensure that attendants are available to pole or row them, and take care that the rice cakes and snacks are not lost.
There is no business [to be done]. One must not wastefully expend the monastery’s permanent provisions of tea, fruit, vegetables, and so forth.
Upon encountering the death of a monk, the funeral director leads the party to the Abbot’s quarters to request the Abbot to perform the *bǐngjù* (flame-handling) ritual.

Next, they proceed to the Meditation Hall to request the *weina* and other masters to recite the liturgy. Once the cremation is completed, the funeral director is again led back to the Abbot’s quarters.

On the day of retirement, one shall perform the ritual of thanksgiving in the meditation hall. All items belonging to the guest quarters must be clearly inventoried according to the register and handed over to the new guest master for custody;
they must not be allowed to become disordered.
Regarding the several points above, those in charge should each examine them closely when faced with specific situations and take the initiative to act accordingly;
there is no need to wait for the Abbot to repeatedly issue oral instructions. Should there be any items that have not been fully detailed, I hope you will always exercise understanding and sympathy.
This is the admonition.
Established by [Name], Abbot of [Mountain Name] Temple, on the [Day] of the [Month] of the [Year].
Instructions for the Bath Master (including the Head of the Inner Latrine):
Without sparing yourself from toil or the extremes of cold and heat, you must visit every household of the donors; this is solely to ensure that their resolve remains firm.
The intent is simply to purify the assembly. Therefore, for every single rinsing and washing, the skillful means are inexhaustible; the resulting merit is likewise unsurpassed.
If these conditions are not fully met, or if the water and heat are improperly managed, how can one avoid manifold distracting thoughts amidst daily activities?
Consequently, I have established several articles specifically as a mirror for the resident quarters, so that those who assume office in the future may also benefit.
Relying upon these, one should practice them so that together they accomplish the sublime task. It is said:

"The commencement period for entering the hall for the *zhai* (fast-day) meal, the dispersal period for exiting the hall for the annual festival *zhai*, and the universal tea service—these should be prepared according to one's means."
During the retreat period, the assembly should prepare cotton cloths, paper, sandals and shoes, utensils, miscellaneous items, and the like. During the retreat period,
incense, oil, lanterns, and so forth for the various locations before the Buddha should be prepared.

The timing for the commencement [of the ritual] should be set. It is appropriate to prepare and present ceremonial robes, tea, and fruit to the Abbot (fangzhang) as well as the head officials (toushou).

The bathing period occurs once every five days, limited to the fifth and tenth days of the lunar month. If the following day is the first or fifteenth (the new or full moon), then the bath is held on the fourteenth or nineteenth.

(Furthermore, when there is a communal labor service or during the summer season, it is appropriate to hold a "burning bath" [hot-water bath]; however, this is not done unless it coincides with the scheduled dates.)
Upon reaching the appointed time, first hang the "Bathing Open" signboard. In the afternoon, arrange the incense table.
When the bathwater is heated, light three sticks of incense and invite the Abbot to enter the bathhouse. Separately, prepare and serve tea and refreshments for his attendance.
When the abbot has finished his bath, he enters the hall to request the bath for the assembly. He then proceeds to the quarters of the various head officials (*śreṣṭhin*).
Once the head officials have finished their baths, he should notify the guest prefect (*karmadāna*) to invite the lay donors (*dānapati*) to bathe.

For the use of the assembly:
once the great assembly has finished bathing, one must wash the basins and ponds clean, sun-dry the cloths and towels, and put away miscellaneous items.
When the period for bathing falls during winter, it is appropriate to install a heating stove to facilitate the warming of robes and clothing.

The supply of hot water must be sufficient, and its temperature should be regulated to be neither too cold nor too hot. Should there be an urgent request from a guest for a bath at night, even if it is outside the designated period, one should still comply with the request.
At dawn and dusk, ensure that the street lamps are properly maintained and illuminated. Be careful with fire, candles, firewood, and ashes.
At dawn and dusk, sweep the latrines clean, empty and rinse the cleansing vessels, and prepare paper sticks in advance for the community's use.
Do not personally misappropriate any items provided for the assembly during this period.
It is appropriate to privately record all the permanent property belonging to this hall in a ledger for the purpose of future inspection.
When among the assembly, one should value broad-mindedness and gentleness. One must not rely on one’s office to act haughtily toward superiors or to oppress subordinates.
On the day one’s term of office ends, all food provided for the community, as well as oil, candles, and other such items, should be delivered to the permanent monastery treasury.
On the day one's term of office expires, one shall clearly inventory all the communal utensils belonging to the monastery as well as miscellaneous items used for the assembly,
and hand them over to the latrine attendant for safekeeping, ensuring that nothing becomes disordered or lost.
Regarding the several points above, those in charge should each examine them closely when faced with specific circumstances and act according to their own capacity.

Senior monks generally appoint those who are experienced in monastic affairs and are diligent and respectful to serve in these roles, for it is because these duties are vital to the abbot’s governance of the assembly. This is improper. Not only does it bring a burden upon the Dharma, but it also fails to provide any support for those who rely on us.

Therefore, I have established several articles to serve as a mirror for our own quarters, so that those who follow in our footsteps may likewise observe and practice them, thereby avoiding the calamity of overturning the cauldron.

Regarding the burning of incense: whenever the Abbot ascends the hall for a formal sermon (*shàngtáng*), a brief discourse (*xiǎocān*), a general lecture (*pǔshuō*), or opens his private quarters (*kāishì*), a fragrant table must be prepared in advance and the incense burner kept ready without fail.

This applies even until the conclusion of the recitation (*niànsòng*) and the dismissal of the assembly (*fàngcān*), as well as during special observances on seasonal anniversaries (*jiélà*) and when visiting renowned and eminent elders from various mountains.

Upon checking in for residence, one should perform the ritual prostrations; the incense burning is conducted in the same manner. On the first and fifteenth days of the month, when the abbot performs the Buddha-worship ceremony, the resident should carry a small box containing incense chips and follow him to attend the formal offering.
At all times, one should wipe clean the ladle and the incense burner, trim pieces from bundles of sandalwood, or polish and brush the staff and sandals.
One should also sun-dry and fumigate the bedding, mats, curtains, seats, couches, and all other such items, ensuring they remain pure and clean.
Sweep [the hall] without negligence.

Regarding formal correspondence: whenever the Abbot presides over the *shàngtáng* (ascending the hall), the *xiǎocān* (small private discourse), opens the meditation room (*kāishì*), or delivers general Dharma talks, as well as for all written inquiries, replies, and verses of praise, record each instance in detail.
If you compose texts on his behalf, ensure that all incoming and outgoing correspondence is first prepared with due care.

Drafts shall be presented for review; only after they have been finalized should action be taken. Should the secretary be temporarily absent, you shall act as his representative for all formal correspondence concerning the mountain gate.
Regarding invitations: whenever the abbot receives visiting guests from various monasteries or venerable elders, you shall take charge of their reception and hospitality.

Regarding the donors (*dānapati*), the host who has issued the invitation, or their special envoys: the guest master (*keshi*) must be instructed in advance to prepare tea and soup, or light refreshments to accompany the meal, according to the circumstances of abundance or scarcity.
Furthermore, when inviting the two orders (*liangxu*) to remain for tea and soup as a gesture of hospitality, these should likewise be prepared in advance.

This applies during the formal lectures (*shangtang*), informal discourses (*xiaocan*), general expositions (*pushe*), the two summer and winter retreats (*zhizhi*), and on the first and fifteenth days of the month (*suowang*). Do not act with haste at the last moment, lest it fail to honor the grand traditions of the monastic community (*sōrin*). Furthermore, when a donor (*dantoku*) or honored guest first arrives at the mountain monastery:
Having completed the audience with the Abbot, one assembles with the various head officers and administrators for a formal reception in the guest hall; those who arrive late are not counted.
On the first and fifteenth days of the month, after everyone has gathered at dawn, if there are donors or honored guests on the mountain, the Guest Master (Kechi) should be informed;

the same applies to formal receptions. Alternatively, if the Rector (Vinaya-master) or the Guest Master does not attend the assembly—either because they are on leave or otherwise absent—[the procedure is adjusted accordingly].

Do not be negligent, lax, or indolent, lest you cause the abbot to lose confidence in you.

Regarding the movement of thought, medicinal decoctions, and the daily offerings of broth and medicine to the Abbot: one must prepare and select the ingredients with meticulous care and discernment regarding their quality.

Depending on the individual's constitutional nature—whether superior or inferior—the treatment may require tonification or depletion. Whether administered as a decoction or a pill, the intensity of the firing process must be adjusted according to the season.
Regarding medical treatment and the administration of medicine, one must know each detail and examine them with care.

Whether it concerns the harmonizing of food and drink—sour, cold, sweet, salty, or bitter—or the seasonal regulations regarding heat and cold, as well as matters such as fanning, shaving, and bathing, one must apply diligent scrutiny according to the occasion so as not to cause any physical imbalance.

Furthermore, in matters of daily conduct and receiving guests, there must be no delay; those selected for these duties must be physically robust, prudent, and sincere, or they may be assisted by others.

The assistant for robes and bowls (*cīvara-pātra-paricāraka*) shall provide care and support to the lay practitioners (*upāsaka*). Should there be a temporary shortage of those to burn incense, receive guests, or manage the assembly, they shall all be assigned to these duties.

They shall establish the ranks of the assembly; this includes the roles of the incense-burner, the scribe, and the guest-receiver (excluding the attendant for the Sacred Sangha [the *śrāvaka-saṃgha*], who walks behind the assembly and is not subject to these regulations).
The duty of an attendant is to dwell closely with the abbot internally and preside over the great assembly externally;

one must take the Buddhas and Patriarchs as one’s heart, maintain solemn harmony between superiors and subordinates, and strive for the ultimate perfection of the Dharma-way so that the mountain gate may thereby flourish in great prosperity.

If, however, one is self-conceited and boastful, failing to treat others with equanimity, then let alone the matter of personal cultivation, even the merit of providing assistance will not be realized.
What need is there for more? Furthermore, as you remain by my side morning and evening, every movement of mind and every stirring of thought is fully understood by me.
If there are instructions to be given, you must apply yourself with care and intimacy; whether matters are great or small, direct or indirect, none shall escape your thorough comprehension.

When facing critical situations, you must act with flexibility and adaptability according to the timing, ensuring that, in sum, you do not contravene the intent of the abbot nor oppose the minds of the assembly. Thus it is. Together.
In serving various administrative offices, it is especially appropriate to maintain harmony and act as each other’s arms and elbows.

Do not harbor feelings of contempt or negligence simply because someone has served for a long time or is a junior colleague. Beyond these few points, there are further detailed instructions that cannot be fully enumerated here;

each of you should examine yourselves and put them into practice without waiting for the abbot to instruct you repeatedly. May those in charge take this to heart and understand its intent. This is the admonition.

The Jiansi (Superintendent) must know that the Sanskrit term *upadhivārika* translates here as "Abbot" (*sizu*) or "Administrator" (*zhishi*). The duty of an administrator is to hold the honor of the master and the love of the assembly as his primary concern.
Therefore, during the flourishing era of the ancient monasteries, the position was frequently offered to the Chief Seat (*shouzuo*) or the West Hall Master (*xitang*).

Record. To fulfill this office, one should be selected from among those who possess seniority in years since ordination (*laba*), are well-versed in affairs, and are renowned for their integrity, capability, and public conscientiousness—those whom the community has long held in high esteem.
Consequently, several articles have been established as a model for this specific department, so that future incumbents may likewise follow them in practice and avoid the risk of failure.
When officials in office come to the mountain monastery, the etiquette for their arrival and departure must first be discussed with the Abbot by the Assistant Director of Guests;
once settled, it may then be carried out.

When an official visiting monk arrives at the mountain monastery, he must first consult with the Chief Steward (*kusi*) and the Guest Master (*chikaku*) regarding the preparation of a certain number of vegetarian offerings (*zhai-zhuan*), as well as a certain number of servings of rice soup, glutinous rice cakes, and fruit. Only after reporting these matters to the Abbot (*fangzhang*) may the proceedings commence.

Furthermore, the furnishings for the official’s quarters—such as beds, curtains, and utensils—as well as incense, candles, firewood, charcoal, and the rice soup and food served upon arrival, must also be arranged in consultation [with the aforementioned officials].

The guest prefect shall attend to them with care; they must not be neglected (if officials are traveling on the road, special tea and meals shall be provided for their accompaniment; such protocols should be adjusted according to the occasion).
When a lay donor (*dānapati*) who is a local official arrives at the mountain, he should be treated with special warmth and courtesy;
one should accompany him for discussions in the morning and evening. If he wishes to visit the various quarters or observe the four sites, he may be escorted there.
Regarding matters of celebration and condolence that ought to be performed by the patrons and donors of this monastery, they shall consult with and report to the Abbot.
As for those patrons and donors whom the monastery must treat with courtesy and respect, whenever they encounter the annual festivals and...
In one's leisure time, it is appropriate to personally visit their homes and inquire after them with great courtesy.
When eminent monks and venerable elders from one's own locality or from various regions arrive at the mountain, they must also be provided with guest quarters and attended to morning and evening.

When a female guest arrives at the mountain, you should provide her with lodging, food, and conversation, treating her with due care; however, you must not become overly intimate with her or manage household affairs on her behalf.

You should regularly visit the treasury office to audit the ledgers of income and expenditure regarding money and grain, ensuring in advance that the annual budget maintains a surplus so as not to fall into temporary destitution.

According to the annual custom, the distribution of rice for the vegetarian feast must be prepared in a timely manner; furthermore, one must invite those designated to receive the rice for the following year.

During the two periods of spring and winter when the retreat is concluded, one should proactively invite the fundraising master (*huazhu*), ensuring that the details are thoroughly verified with reliable merchants before reporting them to the Abbot.
Items for permanent maintenance are often lacking; these should be discussed with the Vice-Abbot.

Funds should be issued to procure them (such as firewood, fodder, salt, oil, beans, sesame, rice, wheat, and so forth—those things that can be raised through casual solicitation should be discussed at the appropriate time, and it is best to assign the community to manage them).

Furthermore, during the fourth lunar month when rain falls incessantly, and during the winter when frost and snow bring severe cold, one must instruct the community in advance to stockpile firewood and fuel to suffice for future use.
Regarding bedding, mats, quilts, cotton fillings, and so forth belonging to the various quarters: if any are damaged, one shall take care of them and request someone to repair them.
As for all property belonging to the permanent monastery (sanghārāma), even if it be as small as a hair’s tip or a tiny grain, it is the share of the monks of the ten directions.

Unless it concerns officials who protect the temple gates, donors, or guests—where it is appropriate to perform the rites of hospitality such as welcoming, seeing off, congratulating, or condoling—all [other matters] must be handled accordingly.
One must not use false pretexts to encroach upon or plunder the community's resources.
In all matters involving the community, one must first consult and report to the Abbot before proceeding; one must not arbitrarily act according to one’s own whims.
Regarding all matters, large or small, entrusted by the Abbot, one must report whether they have been carried out.

When entering or leaving the monastery, one must inform the Abbot, as well as the Head of the Administrative Office (Kusi) and the Guest Master (Zhike), in case urgent business should arise at any time.

To facilitate acting on their behalf, the offices of the estate treasuries must be established with strict impartiality; do not employ private factions that cause resentment among those above and below.

When instructing those under your charge, do not whip or beat them wantonly. Even when it is necessary to administer punishment, censure, or expulsion, you must first submit a report for deliberation and act only after due consideration.
Show them warning through your demeanor; do not indulge in tyranny or violence that might provoke the seeds of contention and disturb the assembly.
Should there be those among the residents of the various quarters who engage in verbal disputes or strife, you must resolve them by appealing to reason and prevent further complications.
The monastic quarters of Tianyuan, Erfang, and others must be visited regularly to offer consolation and encouragement, so that each may remain at peace for the long term.

Should any among them fail to act according to the Dharma or suddenly wish to leave their quarters, they must be skillfully managed and guided so as not to give rise to thoughts of departing elsewhere.
If among the practitioners in the various quarters there are those who cannot endure [the training] and request to resign, one should exhort and comfort them to inspire their aspiration for the Way;
if it becomes unavoidable, then allow them to leave, assigning the *zhikè* (guest prefect) to select others from the assembly to replace them.
When among the assembly, one must be broad-minded and harmonious. One must not rely on one's office to act with arrogance toward superiors or to oppress subordinates.

The administrative officers of each quarter must communicate on matters both great and small; they must not establish separate households or divisions, nor give rise to arbitrary distinctions between "self" and "other."
Those who perform labor or suffer from illness must be provided with care regarding their morning and evening meals, hunger and thirst, and exposure to cold or heat.
Should any member of the assembly harbor a frivolous mind or utter insults, they shall be dealt with through collective deliberation; no one shall dismiss them on their own private authority.

One must not privately take on disciples or indiscriminately bestow Dharma names. Should there be those who sincerely seek refuge, one must consult the guest prefect and report the matter to the Abbot.

Diligently attend to the incense and lamps morning and evening; do not fail in your recitations and chanting. Furthermore, attend the hall for the two daily meals of rice and congee, unless there is a specific reason for otherwise.
When participating in communal labor (*fusshō*), you should follow the assembly, except when there is a specific reason.

Whenever a festival occurs, or during the new and full moon within the prescribed periods, if there is no donor who provides a vegetarian feast and invites the Abbot to ascend the hall for a sermon, then on the afternoon prior to the appointed day, after the Chan Hall has concluded its "small period of silence" (xiaojing), the Abbot shall take his vestments and incense and, together with the various heads of the community, go to pay formal respects and extend the invitation.
On the following morning, he shall invite him again two or three times in the same manner. This applies unless there are other matters requiring his departure.
Then the Kusi (Treasury Office) shall act on behalf of the incumbent.

At the time of the new and full moon, when the great assembly gathers like clouds, they shall chant praises. The official shall leave his seat and offer incense before the Buddha, perform three prostrations with the ritual implements unfolded, and proceed to the position of the Rector (Vina).
There too, he shall leave his seat, unfold his implements, and perform three prostrations. He shall then proceed to the position of Weituo (Vaiśravaṇa).

The procedures for the [reception] hall are also like this, except when there is a specific matter requiring separate departure, in which case the Kusi (Director of the Storehouse) shall act on his behalf.

Whenever there is a communal meal or offering for the Sangha, one must offer incense and perform prostrations before the Buddha; except in cases of specific business, the Kusi shall act on his behalf.

Whenever there is a fixed-term vegetarian meal or tea service, one should join the Guest Prefect (zhikè) in requesting the Abbot (zhùzhí). Except in cases of unavoidable business, the Head of the Treasury (kūsī) shall act as his deputy.

Every night after the minor period of silence has opened, he shall go to the treasury office and, together with the Guest Prefect and the Age-Manager (zhísuì), prepare for and deliberate upon the implementation of the "Bright" (míng) practice.
Regarding matters concerning the temple’s assets: all fields, estates, mountain boundaries, grain rents, written contracts, and so forth must be collected and stored in the treasury,
where they shall be supervised and maintained at all times.
Regarding the cultivation and harvesting of fields and gardens, those in charge of the estates should expedite these tasks at the appropriate times.
All communal utensils belonging to this hall should be privately recorded in a register for the purpose of future inspection.

On the day of retirement, all articles belonging to this quarters, as well as various documents and contracts, shall be clearly inventoried according to the register and handed over to the new head monk (kanjari) for his custody; they must not be allowed to become disordered or confused.
Regarding the several points above, those in charge should each examine them closely when facing actual matters and take the initiative to implement them;

it need not wait for the Abbot to repeatedly issue oral instructions. Should there be any items that are incomplete, I only hope you will exercise understanding and accommodate them as the occasion requires. This is my admonition.

Guidelines for the Assistant Steward.
The ancient regulations referred to this as the *kūtō* (storehouse head); today, various temples call it the *keitō* (treasury head), while in the north it is called the *zaihaku* (treasurer).

In reality, these are all one and the same office; it is essentially the deputy to the *duganshi* (General Supervisor of the Monastery) who shares in the labor. The duty of the Deputy Abbot (*fushi*) requires that his management of receipts and disbursements be impartial and fair.
If he were to hoard the monastery’s permanent assets (*jōjō*) to the detriment of the monks, he would not be acting to protect the community. Therefore, [this office] was established.

These several articles are intended as a model for this very office, so that those who hereafter assume these duties may likewise follow them in practice and avoid the misfortune of failure. Thus it is said.
The treasurer shall manage the permanent funds of cash and silver, carefully recording all income and expenditure in a ledger at the appropriate times.

On the evenings of the fourteenth and thirtieth of each month, he shall have the storekeeper prepare chairs, tables, tea, and refreshments, and invite the Abbot and the heads of the various departments to his quarters.
Calculate the daily expenditures and revenues, and determine the actual amount remaining in the treasury after expenses have been deducted.

Once the calculations are complete, the accountant shall record them in the ledgers, sign the summary sheets, and, if the Abbot is not present, submit them to the Abbot together with the Chief Administrator (Jiansi) and the Guest Master (Zhike).
At the end of the year, a final summary shall again be calculated for each month’s expenditures and revenues.

Record the quantities received; record the quantities remaining in the storehouse after deducting those used. Once the calculations are complete, enter them into the registers and submit the receipts accordingly.
For other items such as rice, wheat, cloth, silk, and the five flavors, their entry and exit must likewise be recorded and reported to the calendar at all times.
For the purpose of accounting,
one must keep one's mind focused on the money, silver, cloth, silk, grain, and other goods within the storehouse day and night,
so as to prevent any loss.
If storehouses are neglected and leaky, allowing rats and birds to cause damage and waste, or if rice, wheat, and all other goods become damp and moldy,
they must be promptly disposed of if they are not properly stored or guarded according to the rules.
The storehouse manager shall issue sufficient silver for procurement expenses. He must consult with the Abbot’s Assistant (Jiansi) or the Guest Master (Zhike) and report to the Abbot.
He must then report back on whether the various matters entrusted by the Abbot have been carried out as instructed.
The administrative officers of each quarter must coordinate matters both great and small; they must not establish separate households or divisions, nor give rise to feelings of "self" versus "other.
When living among the community, one must be broad-minded and harmonious; one must not rely on the authority of one's office to be haughty toward superiors or oppressive toward subordinates.
During the two periods for the morning and evening gruel, one must attend the hall; one may not pursue private interests at the expense of the community, except when there is a specific reason.

The upper and lower storehouse managers must consult with the Chief Administrator (Jian-si) and the Guest Master (Zhi-ke) to select those who possess diligence and capability, who are able to exercise discretion and adaptability, and who maintain integrity and conscientiousness.

The storekeeper must be treated with due care. In all matters, one must deliberate with impartiality; one must not harbor grudges or yield to private interests. No one shall arbitrarily dismiss or revoke the position of others.

Regarding all property belonging to the permanent monastery, even the smallest fraction—down to a hair’s breadth or a grain of dust—is the share of the Sangha from the ten directions. If it is not [the property of] the temple...

Regarding those who guard the gates, government officials, donors, guests, and those with whom one must perform formal social duties such as welcoming, seeing off, celebrating, or offering condolences:
none of these may be used as a pretext for fraudulent accounting or embezzlement.

Regarding household goods and daily utensils, one must aim for frugality and fairness; they must not be given away lightly or spent wastefully, thereby causing loss to the permanent property of the monastery.
In all matters, one should take the protection and care of the permanent property as one's primary concern, yet one must not be so rigidly attached as to diminish the provisions of the assembly.
Even if one enters with heavy items and exits with light ones, it may provoke public criticism and resentment.

Regarding the fruits and provisions held in common for the monastery, one must not yield to private interests by selling them to the community (though selling such provisions to the community is a matter of human convenience;

however, the primary requirement for hosting guests is to ensure their needs are met. Furthermore, trading involves much hassle and inevitably invites complaints regarding discrepancies in quantity and price. Therefore, it is better to simply eliminate this practice).
Regarding items required for the sustenance of sick monks, they shall be provided promptly as needed; no hardship or difficulty shall be permitted.
As for the tea, fruits, and provisions required for the quarters of the Head Seat (Shouzuo) and the West Hall (Xitang), the storekeeper (Kuzi) shall be ordered to prepare and deliver them.

Whenever there is a regular custom requiring the provision of tea and refreshments, they shall be provided immediately. Furthermore, the tea and refreshments used during the period of the precept-retreat shall follow the same precedent.

The monastery administration shall provide rewards for the administrative officers, ensuring that the storekeeper is informed and that attendants are assigned to manage and oversee the distribution of food and provisions.
Whenever the assembly acts as the host for a transformation ceremony and the master emerges from the mountain, all offerings and ritual gifts should be set aside in advance.
Whether entering or exiting at dawn or dusk, the storekeeper must be ordered to guard them; if no one is present in the storeroom, it is inappropriate to leave lightly.
The storehouse lacks vegetables, fruits, oil, salt, sugar, beans, utensils, and miscellaneous items;
these should be prepared in advance so as not to result in shortages when needed at the last moment.
Regarding daily household necessities such as fermented paste, soy sauce, rice vinegar, and bean oil, one should promptly request those who are experienced to assist in their preparation.
As for items stored in the larder, such as cakes and pastries that ought to be made by oneself, these should be prepared at the appropriate times.
Regarding the side dishes for guests kept in the storehouse: those requiring the five flavors of fragrant pepper and other ingredients shall be prepared with care by the storekeeper.
When a vegetarian offering is made, the storekeeper shall arrange the fruit offerings before the Buddha and at the positions of the abbot and others, exactly according to established custom.
If a donor desires them to be abundant and aesthetically pleasing, it is appropriate to add further items accordingly.

When a donor provides a vegetarian feast and prepares the ritual offerings, they shall be brought inside by the attendant of the hall. The quality and quantity of these items shall follow the established precedent;
however, if the donor has a specific intention to add extra items, this shall be treated as a separate case.

When a donor provides a vegetarian feast and distributes alms (*dakṣiṇā*), if the guest prefect is busy with his duties, it is appropriate for him to act as a deputy (furthermore, regarding the distribution of alms, there are instances of equal division and those that are not;
one should exercise discretion according to the circumstances).

On a certain day, a donor provides a vegetarian feast (*zhāi*). Although it is known that guests have been invited in advance, the affairs of the feast must nevertheless be entrusted to the guest master (*zhikē shàng*).
Whenever the annual festivals, the new and full moons, or the time for inviting the Abbot to ascend the hall occurs, the storekeeper (*kùzǐ*) shall first...

The Abbot shall personally arrange the incense and candles according to the established custom (if the Abbot’s quarters are far removed from the storehouse, it is permissible for the Guest Master to dispatch an attendant to manage them;
there is no need for mutual deference or insistence on protocol).

When the Chief Administrator (Jianyuan) has other duties and is absent, he shall act as the officiant on all occasions when the Abbot is invited to ascend the hall for the New Year, the first day of the month, or the full and new moon;

when incense is offered before the Buddha during these monthly services; and when incense is offered during the communal meals of the monastery. On all such occasions, the Chief Administrator shall serve in his stead.
When the Chief Administrator (Jianyuan) has other duties and is absent, if the monastery (changzhu) serves a meal or tea, he should join the Guest Master (Zhike) in requesting the Abbot (Fangzhang).
Regarding the annual custom of distributing rice for meals, he should manage these affairs in a timely manner and invite those who will receive the rice distribution for the following year.

When the position of the Administrative Head (Jianyuan) is vacant, or when he must leave on official business, matters such as estate taxes and deeds, the management of income and expenditures, welcoming and seeing off guests,

and the dispatching of personnel for celebrations or condolences— indeed, all essential affairs at various locations— should be discussed with the Guest Prefect (Zhike), and they shall attend to these duties jointly.
All utensils and articles within the storehouse shall be recorded in a register for the purpose of inspection.
All utensils and articles in all large and small quarters shall be recorded in a general register for the purpose of inspection.
On the day of retirement, one must request the various heads of the community to audit the ledgers and accounts.
All items, including money, silver, cloth, grain, and all utensils and provisions, shall be clearly inventoried item by item and handed over to the new assistant administrator for custody;
they must not be allowed to become disordered.
Regarding the several points above, those in charge should each examine them closely when the occasion arises and take the initiative to implement them;

it is not necessary to wait for the Abbot to repeatedly issue verbal instructions. Should there be any items that are incomplete, I only hope you will exercise understanding and accommodate them as the situation requires. This is my admonition.

Regarding the duties of the *Dianzuo* (Chief Cook):

to establish one's virtue amidst the dense thicket of worldly affairs, nothing is more significant than providing for one’s livelihood through the support of offerings. Therefore, one who presides over the kitchen of the clouds...
The Administrator (*ren*) is one who can harmonize the various voices [of the community] so that the hundred blessings are complete.
If the six flavors are not refined or the three virtues are not provided, then it will not serve the assembly during the two meal times.
Therefore, I have established several articles as a mirror for this primary hall, hoping that those who assume office hereafter may follow them in practice and avoid any faults or transgressions.
In all offerings, one must ensure that the materials are pure and refined, the five flavors are harmoniously blended, and the raw and cooked portions are appropriately prepared;
one must not be negligent or allow such matters to cause concern among the assembly.

Offerings for the midday meal before the Buddha shall be prepared according to one's means, whether abundant or frugal, and must be arranged with uniformity; they must not be uneven or irregular, as this has become a long-standing tradition.

When honored guests arrive at the mountain, the preparation of vegetables and greens must be handled with particular diligence and supervision; it must not be treated with the same casual attitude as that accorded to ordinary visitors.
It is therefore permissible to arrange the seating according to the available space.
One should prepare guest dishes in advance to guard against unexpected visitors arriving at any time.
Whenever there are leftover vegetables or remaining offerings that can be shared among the assembly, they should be distributed; do not hoard them so that they become stale.
This leads to spoilage.

Regarding the heavy task of serving the assembly, when it comes to the vegetables required for morning and evening meals, one must prepare them skillfully and harmoniously, ensuring that no resentment is caused.
If any member of the assembly, braving cold and heat, seeks sour and pungent broth, one should provide it on their behalf.
If any member of the assembly has no business but demands vegetables indiscriminately, one must not give them lightly.
Oils, sauces, the five flavors, and so forth, should be collected and stored in the kitchen. One must not take them for private use or consume them recklessly based on personal whims.

With the intention of protecting and cherishing the communal property (*sangha-ratna*), one must not secretly appropriate vegetables or privately prepare food and drink for the purpose of catering to personal favors or social obligations.
During the two meal periods, the rice porridge and cooked rice in the kitchen must not differ from that of the assembly.
The pots and stoves must be kept clean, and one must exercise extreme care with fire and candles. (From the preceding section to this point is a supplementary notice for the case.)

The administrative officers of each quarters must coordinate matters both great and small; they must not establish separate households or divisions to foster arbitrary distinctions between "self" and "other.
When dwelling among the assembly, one should value broad-mindedness and harmony; one must not rely on one's office to act haughtily toward superiors or to oppress subordinates.
Those of equal rank at the same desk should deliberate together; do not stubbornly insist on your own views or engage in mutual resentment and contention.
Keep in mind that both labor and rest must be shared equally; do not rely on your office to remain idle yourself.

When a donor provides a vegetarian feast (*zhāi*), all funds for flour and silver shall be distributed according to their amount, apportioned based on the rank and responsibility of each position (for example, if one copper coin is collected, five parts go to the supervisor, three to the cook, and two to the fire-attendant; however, if there is excessive labor, slight adjustments may be made, with each person determining the appropriate measure according to the circumstances).

At the fifth watch, when the bell for the report sounds, rise early in time to await the signal gong. Should anyone fail to do so, they shall enter the hall at night to perform bows of inquiry in their respective places.
Regarding the two periods for passing through the hall, one must ensure that the pace is neither too slow nor too hurried, but remains within the proper measure.
Whenever encountering public affairs, one should follow the assembly, except when the matters are so numerous as to preclude such consideration.
All items belonging to the monastery’s permanent inventory held within one's own quarters should be privately recorded in a register for the purpose of future reference and inspection.

On the day of retirement, all the utensils and belongings belonging to this quarters shall be clearly accounted for according to the inventory register and handed over to the new chief cook (dianzuo) for custody;
they must not be allowed to become disordered or lost.
Regarding the several points above, those in charge should each examine them closely when faced with specific matters and put them into practice.
Should there be any items that are incomplete, we only hope for your understanding and accommodation at all times. This is the instruction.
