The *zhisui* (Director of Affairs) is responsible for all administrative duties; thus he is named the *zhisui*. Those who hold this office must value public-mindedness and diligence in accomplishing tasks.
With the thought that toil and ease must always be shared equally, if the quarters are not maintained and the utensils are not provided,
the way of settling the assembly is lost. Therefore, I have established several articles specifically as a mirror for this own hall,
so that those who later assume office may rely upon and practice them, ensuring there is no anxiety over the failure of affairs.

Whenever halls, pavilions, or quarters suffer from leaks, or when doors, windows, walls, or embankments collapse or crumble, one must promptly inform the Abbot so that he may organize the laborers for repair.
Do not procrastinate until the days pass by, thereby leaving a burden for future generations.
There shall always be labor involving various tasks of earth and wood;
you shall lead the many workmen and supervise them morning and evening, calculating the daily progress, the silver required, and the silver expended, recording these privately in a ledger.

This is for the purpose of settlement. If it involves major construction or renovation, the matter is highly complex; one must immediately consult with the Abbot to increase the number of personnel to jointly manage it.

Every night, after the "Small Silence" (xiaojing) has concluded, go to the storehouse to work together with the Chief Administrator (jianyuan) and the Guest Master (zhike) to deliberate on and carry out the necessary arrangements.
Regarding matters for the following day:

as there will be heavy tasks requiring a large number of laborers, those who wish to provide tea, snacks, and noodles as rewards should take notice of this in advance and consult with the storehouse officials and guest masters.

Among the craftsmen, both great and small, those who do not work diligently shall be dismissed for their idleness; do not permit such parasitic consumption that devours wealth and harms the public interest.
As for the sowing, planting, and harvesting of fields and gardens, those in charge of the estates must ensure these tasks are carried out with timely urgency.
Fields, gardens, and dwellings; oil-mills, flour-mills, and water-mills; as well as horses, pack animals, boats, and carts—all must be maintained and repaired in a timely manner.
Furthermore, one should appropriately patrol, guard, and provide warning against fire, arson, and bandits.
Hoes, saws, axes, hatchets, raincoats, straw hats, poles, ropes, and other miscellaneous items used must be placed within the storehouse;
let the storekeeper take charge of them. Should any become damaged or decayed, he shall be instructed to repair them promptly.
Within the storehouse, one shall inventory all movable utensils and effects, ordering the storekeeper to record each item individually for the purpose of future reference.
Within the storehouse, regarding the daily use of utensils and equipment, if any items are missing and require purchase, one must inform the storehouse supervisor (kusi) to procure them.
When boats enter or depart, one must supervise the loading and unloading of goods, as well as instruct the guards on how to secure and release the mooring ropes.
Regarding matters such as protection against floods and droughts during the two seasons, one must report back on whether all tasks entrusted by the Abbot—whether large or small—are being carried out.
The administrative officers of the various quarters must coordinate both major and minor affairs; they must not establish separate households or factions, nor give rise to mutual divisiveness.
One must not exclusively pursue one's own duties while neglecting public affairs or evading responsibilities, thereby causing dissatisfaction among one's colleagues.
When presiding over a group, one should value broad-mindedness and harmony; one must not rely on one’s position to act haughtily toward superiors or to oppress subordinates.
If there are those who commit offenses against me, I shall consider their hardships and must not harbor resentment or private grudges;
I will certainly remove them from their positions before I cease.

In assigning tasks and issuing orders, all matters of reward and punishment must be handled with propriety; do not yield to favoritism or partiality, thereby causing resentment among those above and below.

On the day of the communal labor (pǔqǐng), a notice shall be posted in advance, with the following written on its side: "At such-and-such place, for such-and-such task," followed by the time for the communal rice gruel and meal.
When this is finished, the long gong is struck and the standing call is given. For those who do not attend, all parties must jointly urge them to hasten.

Regarding work assignments, going out on the slopes, and collecting firewood during summer and winter, the designated number of monks from the Meditation Hall must report to the Rector (Weina), and the designated number of monks from the Guest Hall must report to the Hall Master (Tangzhu).
No one shall arbitrarily assign duties; as for the other large and small administrative offices...
When entering the quarters, one should take the lead in the rotation of the duty station.

When the community is called to work outside the monastery, one must take the initiative with one's own body; one must not shirk or go against the assembly. This excludes matters of trivial detail, which need not be discussed.
Whenever a monk’s illness becomes terminal, one must first prepare firewood and fuel.

Upon the arrival of his final moments, the various attendants are notified in advance to arrange the funeral niche, the altar for the deceased, and to provide offerings of food, tea, fruit, incense, and paper money.

All personal belongings belonging to the deceased monk shall be inventoried together with the Guest Prefect and placed in vacant storage areas of the monastery; furthermore, a group of monks shall be assigned to manage the funeral procession.
Attend to the water and fire, as well as the lifting of the shrine-casket (*kaṅ*). Furthermore, hang the name tablet for the deceased. Wait until the assembly has finished their morning gruel;
then, after chanting, escort [the remains] out to the cremation site. The abbot stands firm and, having offered greetings, passes the torch.

Awaiting the commencement of the ritual service, on the following day, he leads the chief mourner to collect the bones using ceramic vessels. These are stored, sealed, and then placed in various locations.
The private chamber is for the purpose of entering the stupa.

When auctioning the belongings of a deceased monk, the two orders of officials must jointly preside over the proceedings. (Regarding these two matters—funerary rites and the auction of goods—the *Baizhang Qinggui* states:)

This has been recorded in great detail; however, fearing it might be overly cumbersome, it is difficult to cite everything in full. For the time being, I have recorded the general outline of what is currently in common practice, so as to facilitate provisional application.
All the permanent utensils and furnishings belonging to this quarters shall be privately recorded in a register for the purpose of future reference.
Regarding the Qingming festival for the sweeping of ancestral stupas— namely the abbot’s stupa, the general stupas, and so forth—

one should instruct the attendants in advance to clear away weeds and sweep the altar sites clean, and to open the burial vaults to collect and enshrine the remains of deceased monks, whether the stones have collapsed or the plaster has crumbled.
Maintain and repair [the facilities] according to the season; do not allow them to fall into ruin.

On the day of relinquishing office, one must clearly inventory all household utensils and items belonging to the administrative quarters according to the register and hand them over to the newly appointed *zhisui* (administrative officer) for custody; they must not be left in disorder.
Regarding the several points above, those in charge should each examine them closely when faced with specific matters and act proactively;

there is no need to wait for frequent verbal instructions from the Abbot. Should there be any items that are not fully detailed, we hope you will exercise understanding and adapt accordingly at all times.
This is the admonition.
The Guidelines for the Two Orders of the Monastic Community, established by the Abbot [Name] of Mount [Name], Japan, in the spring month of the Jīmǎo year of the Chóngzhēn era (1639). (End)
